articles.title: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、AI agent & application
articles.summary: As millions embrace personal AI assistants, a new benchmark reveals that even the most advanced AI models struggle to complete everyday tasks reliably and safely without introducing potential new problems.
articles.full_text:
AI companies have spent the last couple of months marketing personal AI agents as tools to take over the digital drudgery of human existence — and millions have been sold on the vision, handing over their shopping schedules, travel plans, and everyday responsibilities to AI assistants.

But new research suggests that even the most advanced AI models struggle to reliably and safely navigate the messy details of people’s lives.

According to ShellBench, a new benchmark for everyday agent work, even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta failed more than a third of the time.

Across all models tested, 15.7% of attempts failed at least one safety requirement, often leading to unintended consequences.  ShellBench was developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley, drawing on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to see how agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them.  The research comes as personal AI assistants are finding new popularity among developers, with Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic all fighting for a piece of the market with Muse, Dots , and Claude Duet , respectively.

In October, Meta said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up its personal AI agent, Muse, within six weeks of launch, with about a quarter using it daily.

That number is expected to grow as Meta implants Muse directly into Instagram DMs .

Despite growing popularity among consumers, we still have little evidence about how reliable AI personal assistant products actually are.

ShellBench suggests that the unreliable nature of most everyday data sources still causes problems for many state-of-the-art systems.

A successful agent should be able to navigate messy personal workspaces containing emails, calendar entries, spreadsheets, receipts, chat logs, outdated information, and phishing attempts, and figure out which information is relevant, what is private, and how to deliver the requested outcome without creating new problems.  It seems many of today’s AI agents are still not up to the task.

Not only did even the highest-performing agents frequently fail to meet the requirements of a task, but they also lacked consistency.

When researchers ran each task three times under identical conditions, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the highest-scoring model, nailed all three attempts less than half the time.

For autonomous assistants that are meant to run in the background without supervision, it’s a problem if users need to run an agent multiple times to get a result they trust.

Additionally, about 10% of otherwise correct attempts failed at least one safety criterion.

Across the models and harnesses tested, agents failed to, for example, adequately account for a child’s school pickup 79.5% of the time.

When handling laptop custody records, agents failed a requirement to identify and withhold a sensitive bank upload token in 18.6% of attempts.

In another task, agents recommended duplicate or incorrect invoice payments 40.3% of the time.

The findings highlight a major issue for users adopting consumer personal AI assistants, namely that there’s always a risk that an agent can create more headaches in the course of trying to fulfill an otherwise ordinary request.

While AI benchmarks have largely focused on coding, professional work, or testing on specific tasks, ShellBench is attempting to evaluate how models perform on multi-step personal tasks within different agent harnesses — the software that controls how a model accesses information, uses tools, and takes actions.  While the researchers found model choice had a greater overall impact on performance than harness choice, among the more capable models, AI agent performance became more dependent on the harness.

For example, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra outperformed Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 when operating within the Pi harness, but it performed worse when both models were tested within Claude Code.  Meta’s Muse Wonder Full scored 56% in Pi, but only 38.1% in Claude Code.

Meta’s Muse Wonder 1.0, meanwhile, averaged a success rate of 39.7% across the five harnesses tested.

Notably, while the researchers tested models from Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic, they didn’t evaluate them within the native harnesses of Muse, Dots, or Claude Duet, so the results may not be representative of the experience millions of consumers are having with the product today.  TechCrunch has reached out to Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, and the researchers in the study.

articles.title: Maple raises $5.3M to build AI products that protect your data, even from itself
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: The startup's encrypted AI architecture is designed to prevent even the company itself from accessing users' private data.
articles.full_text:
As AI assistants evolve into more capable agents that can access our files, emails, calendar, browser, and more, the amount of trust we’re expected to place in AI companies is growing.

One startup called Maple , co-founded by a former Apple engineer who worked on privacy-preserving technologies, is taking a different approach with its AI app, where users’ data remains private — even from the company itself. “We wanted to build something that was not only encrypted but also could be proven, and that people could go look at the open-source code, and then they could look at what we call trusted execution environments,” explains Maple co-founder and CEO Mark Suman . “They can look at and verify the code that’s running on our servers, so they don’t really have to take our word for it.” “They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled,” he adds.

The idea of trust is Maple’s larger theme, as the startup proposes that there’s a way to build an AI app where consumers don’t have to trade privacy for convenience, as its competitors often require with their invasive privacy policies and data collection practices , and sometimes even training on users’ personal data .

Instead of asking users to trust that Maple won’t misuse their personal data, it’s attempting to build a business where it can’t access that data in the first place.

Like other AI apps on the market, Maple allows users to engage in a chat experience where they ask questions and get answers.

Meanwhile, its newly launched desktop app, Maple Work , offers a more agentic experience where the AI can control your computer, work with your files and apps, and control your browser to get online tasks handled.

With the company’s recently closed $5.3 million round, it’s moving on to its next product — a cloud-based agent that will be able to continue its work even if your computer isn’t on.

This addition would make Maple more competitive with other popular consumer AI services, like Meta’s Muse , Instinct , and other AI agents that work over chat.

The oversubscribed seed round was led by Epic Ventures, with participation from Draper Associates, Planetary VC, and Epoch VC, and follows a pre-seed angel round of under a million.

Maple plans to raise a Series A in the first half of 2027, given the investor interest.

Suman, who previously spent six years at Apple, already had a background where AI and privacy overlapped, he tells TechCrunch.

At Apple, he worked on AI and machine learning with a particular focus on computer vision.

Given Apple’s stance on consumer privacy, the challenge he faced was building products that would protect people’s identity while benefiting from computer vision techniques.

His co-founder, Anthony Ronning (CTO), has a background in defense tech, security, and networking.

Ronning started the company that later became Maple AI back in 2023, initially as a privacy-focused fintech.

When Suman teamed up with Ronning in August 2024, the idea to create Maple AI was born.

The following January, the product became available to the public as a mobile app.

The app offers a familiar interface for those used to AI chatbots, but under the hood it runs a variety of open models, including versions of DeepSeek , Kimi , GLM , Inkling from Thinking Machines, Google’s Gemma , and OpenAI’s GPT OSS .

Users can pick and choose the models they want or, for a simpler experience, just toggle between a quick model and the more powerful one.

The models themselves run inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) — meaning a server with hardware encryption on it — within a U.S.-based data center. (Maple also offers support for European customers through a partner that runs its server in Europe.) “We actually don’t have access to [the data] while it’s inside the TEE,” explains Suman. “The data gets encrypted first on your device using a unique password that’s only known by you, the user — we don’t have access to it.

It then goes into this TEE, and it gets decrypted inside there.

The AI does its thing, and then it re-encrypts it with your password and sends it back to you,” he continues. “So we provide an end-to-end experience that’s very easy for the user, but we actually don’t have access to the raw data as it’s in flight or even when it’s at rest,” he adds.

This allows Maple to protect its users’ data, even from outsiders — like if hackers breached its system or the government came with a subpoena, for instance.

All it could do would be to hand over an encrypted file. “We just simply don’t want access to it,” Suman says of customers’ data. “That’s not part of our business model.

And we also don’t want it to be part of our threat model.” With the new desktop app, Maple is looking to small businesses that may want to benefit from AI without the data privacy risks.

Inside the app, there’s an integration store where users can connect with other apps, like their Gmail or calendar.

The desktop app can also spin up a subagent that works inside another AI app you may have on your desktop, like Claude, Codex, or others that support the Agent Client Protocol (ACP).

This allows customers to use their preferred AI app for specific tasks, without having to give it all their information — just what’s needed for the given task.

Next year, Maple plans to enter the enterprise market with pilot work, where it will offer its own version of zero data retention. (Maple doesn’t retain most of the customers’ data, but when it has to, that data is encrypted.) It’s now in the process of completing SOC 2 compliance and security audits to get ready for this expansion.

The company declined to share its registered customer numbers but noted it’s seen 60x growth over the past three months, as people have been looking for ways to increase their security with AI.

Maple currently generates revenue via subscriptions, which are comparable to those from other AI model providers.

Its Pro plan is $20 per month, and it offers two Max plans, Max and Max Plus, at $100 and $200 per month, respectively.

The Austin- and San Francisco-based startup is a team of four and is actively hiring.

articles.title: Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: Anthropic’s post-IPO slump could put pressure on AI startup valuations.
articles.full_text:
In Brief Posted: 10:30 AM PST · November 24, 2026 Marina Temkin Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83 , trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.

Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value.

The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector.

The dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share .

If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies.

Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday.

Nvidia fell more than 7% by midday, giving back some of the more than 30%-plus gain it posted Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.

articles.title: Meta brings its Muse AI assistant directly into Instagram DMs
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、AI agent & application
articles.summary: The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent.
articles.full_text:
Instagram users can now chat with Meta’s AI agent Muse in a DM thread, the company announced on Tuesday.

The social media network says users can chat with Muse to get more context about a post, place, or product they come across, or catch up on conversations they may have missed in their other DMs.

The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent.

It also reflects the growing competition among tech companies to make AI assistants a part of users’ everyday digital lives.

By embedding Muse directly into Instagram, Meta is making it easier for users to access the AI agent, while also giving Muse access to a platform where users already discover products, places, and content.

Users can share Instagram posts with Muse and ask it to take action, such as adding a coffee shop to their Mexico City itinerary or finding a Black Friday deal on a pair of shoes.

Meta notes that conversations with Muse on Instagram will appear as a side chat in the main Muse app.

Muse in Instagram DMs will begin rolling out on Tuesday for iOS and Android users in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore.

Meta also announced that users can now do more with the posts and reels they’ve bookmarked on Instagram.

For example, they can ask Muse to organize their saved content into custom folders, known as Collections.

They could also ask Muse to turn a recipe video into a grocery list, turn the travel content from their favorite travel creators into an itinerary for an upcoming trip, or have Muse send them outfit ideas based on fashion reels they’ve collected.

Starting Tuesday, when users save a post on Instagram, they will see a prompt for Muse to organize it for them.

This feature is launching in the U.S. and Canada.

Meta says that users remain in control of their Muse experience on Instagram.

Nothing is shared, published, or sent without their approval, and they can ask Muse to forget information or undo actions at any time.

articles.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
articles.summary: The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI "in ways that may not be apparent to users." In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times' photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh […]
articles.full_text:
AI News Tech The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’ An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’ by Emma Roth Nov 24, 2026, 4:09 PM UTC Link Share Gift Photo: Marcin Golba / NurPhoto via Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads , two of the Times ’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.” Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools.

The November update cited by the NYT ’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view , which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar.

It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.

It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite.

This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production.

For a newsroom like the Times , where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust.

Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.” Related Adobe is going all in on agentic AI Photoshop, Lightroom, and Premiere are making it easier to remove things In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps , which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features.

The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads.

NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge , which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.

It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to.

Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for more information.

Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT .
